original_decision: When an archival conversion removes a forbidden action, promote its surviving Next subtree into its position; where the holder accepts only one action, retain the first survivor and attach the remaining sequence to its Next.
reason: This follows Table 196's required post-action sequence and Note 1's recursive order. The archival rewrite preserves the permitted actions after a removed Launch instead of losing them. Current source implements promotion and the integration test checks that a Named NextPage action remains after Launch removal.

This is a writer-side preservation test; reader action order is separately tested in action.rs. Parent correction: the test only searches output bytes for NextPage; it does NOT verify that OpenAction reaches it, nor ordering of multiple survivors. Meaningful preservation proof remains missing.
spec_or_external_sources: Effective EC3 §12.6.2 Table 196 /Next and Note 1; ISO 19005-2 6.5.1 and ISO 19005-4 6.6.1 as stated in ADR 1175.

original_decision: Refuse conversion when a shared action object is reached from distinct positions whose removals require different Next tails, rather than cloning or choosing one tail.
reason: The archive writer cannot represent two distinct successor sequences in one shared dictionary without changing identity or structure. However, the reader's global visited set independently deduplicates all repeated references, including non-cyclic siblings. Table 196 does not explicitly define the execution multiplicity of a repeated object reference; the sibling occurrence test draft probes this reader issue and does not invalidate the archive writer refusal rationale. Parent: conflicting tails refusal is a conservative project preservation choice; cloning could represent both sequences technically, so inability is conditional on the no-cloning fence rather than a PDF-format impossibility.
current_code_evidence: crates/pdf-transform/src/archive/actions.rs records one Next per object and refuses conflicting tails; crates/pdf-model/src/action.rs::push uses a global BTreeSet<ObjectId>.
test_evidence: Archive test a_launch_action_goes_and_the_actions_behind_it_stay covers promotion but not conflicting shared tails. Scratch tests.rs has a full valid-PDF positive control and repeated-reference discriminator; not run in this audit. Parent repeated-reference regression executed and FAILS; reader occurrence loss is separate from writer policy.
spec_or_external_sources: Effective EC3 §12.6.2 Table 196 and Note 1 distinguish ordered array execution from self-referential-cycle handling.

Corrupt compressed bytes can also yield altered decoded bytes before failure, so consumed bits do not prove original producer bytes. Type 3 loading returns Font::Type3 from the referenced dictionary; text/show dispatches its encoded codes through that font's CharProcs.

The current `Scripts` level permits that script to execute at on, warn, and answered-ask; off-by-default and process confinement do not establish a blanket permission to reorder supported actions when the runner is supplied. A100/A286 changed the scope premise by making execution required at supplied-runner sites, with no order exception.

The new test draft uses a reversed JavaScript->SetOCGState positive control and a SetOCGState->JavaScript expected-order case. The runner reads `event.document.layers[0].on` through the public API, and final Query::Layers verifies the viewer-side action. Root promoted and ran the test: ordering assertion fails after the reverse-order and final-state controls pass.

Table 74 requires pattern Resources; the missing-entry reader route uses an empty dictionary, and neither §7.8.3 nor EC3 Issue #128 states a pattern fallback. The archive assignment is nevertheless reachable and writes the page dictionary into a referenced pattern lacking Resources, which can make a page-only XObject name resolve and add marks. ADR 2500's blanket unchanged-resolution assertion is therefore false for malformed pattern inputs. This does not imply ISO requires a reader to reject or repair the malformed source.

original_decision: Represent integer, real, and boolean values distinctly; integer arithmetic remains integer when representable, promotes to real on overflow.
reason: PLRM3 describes polymorphic numeric result types and explicitly states add result is integer only when both operands are integers and the result is within integer range; abs minimum integer becomes real. The implementation's checked promotion matches these obligations for covered arithmetic operators.

The parse-time analysis rejects cases it proves; unknown dataflow remains a known implementation coverage limit and runtime coerces booleans. original_decision: Treat an empty stack pop as integer zero so hand-written documents that underflow and still render can produce a result; avoid per-pixel refusal/report cost.
reason: The witness and performance concern remain evidence for recovery policy, but the historical premise that the clause provides no operative semantics is superseded by PLRM3: operator entries require stackunderflow. The current zero fallback is therefore a semantic gap for invalid functions, not a standards-derived choice. No correction is proposed absent an approved evaluator error/report design and separate measurement of the affected population and cost.
current_code_evidence: EMPTY_STACK is Integer(0); apply_operator::pop substitutes it and several stack operators return defaults/no-op on insufficient stack. Function::eval is infallible.
test_evidence: an_empty_operand_stack_reads_as_the_integer_zero and an_underflowing_program_yields_a_value_rather_than_panicking pin recovery behavior. They are evidence of current policy, not normative conformance tests. No invalid behavior is asserted as desired in the new drafts.
spec_or_external_sources: PLRM3 §8.2 stack operator entries list stackunderflow. ISO §7.10.5.3 declares errors for output count/type mismatch and stack overflow. Annex I concerns newer versions/extensions and does not generally excuse defined operator outcomes.
changed_premise: The normative PLRM3 text is now in hand, showing the empty-stack behavior is specified as an error.
remaining_work: Measure affected valid corpus documents, rendering impact, report cost and API options before deciding whether/how to correct the error gap.
parent_qualification: Recovery value and reporting are separate decisions. Retaining zero as a recovery value can be reasonable; silent recovery is not established as normative conformance. Historical population/cost not rerun.

original_decision: Use sign-preserving right shifts as a value-based choice because ISO 32000-2 did not state integer width.
reason: PLRM3 p539 requires all inserted bits to be zero. Its warning that arithmetic equivalence holds only for positive input explains logical shift, not permission to sign-extend negative values. Current checked_shr on signed i32 violates this for valid negative inputs. A width-independent runtime test verifies that a right-shifted negative value is nonnegative.
current_code_evidence: Operator::Bitshift uses checked_shr for negative shifts and sign extension for negative values; positive shift bits lost at machine-width boundaries are currently zeroed by checked_shl behavior.
test_evidence: crates/pdf-colour/tests/calculator_operators_spec_audit.rs:7PASS1FAIL; negative right-shift assertion fails after positive control. bitshift-isolated-baseline.log and bitshift-isolated-logical-shift-experiment.log establish the causal difference.
spec_or_external_sources: PLRM3 §8.2 bitshift p.539; ISO §B.3 informative summary.

remaining_work: Production correction and affected existing sign-preserving tests remain for a later fix task; audit changes only tests. Isolated logical-shift experiment passes all8 operator tests, compared with7PASS1FAIL baseline, and was restored.
parent_correction: The text defines zero-fill for bit shifts. Its arithmetic warning explains that logical right shift differs from signed division; it does not make negative inputs undefined. Existing sign-preserving tests lock a departure. Public width-independent regression reproduces it on valid input. No production fix performed.

decision_id: treat dialog preferences as editable defaults; report rather than obey Enforce
original_decision: GTK opens its print dialog on Table 147's values and lets the person change them. Enforce is reported, not obeyed, because a document telling the reader what may be changed is a restriction owned by the reader.
reason: This is an explicit documented departure: ADR 1180 already records that Enforce is reported rather than obeyed under the project’s reader-owned restriction policy. The audit does not reclassify that known choice as an undiscovered implementation bug or require owner reapproval. It does establish the actual conflict precisely: Table 147/148 requires later UI selections not to override an enforced scaling value; Qt shows an editable scaling choice, sets its opening value from the preference, then reads the changed value after acceptance. GTK initializes settings and has no later scaling-reapply callback, but source alone does not prove its native UI exposes an editable scale control.
test_evidence: Existing Defaults test checks the valid Enforce condition and status note; Qt host test ends before the native dialog. Qt C++ source proves an available override path via an editable combo and later currentData read. No test needed to rediscover the recorded policy choice; if the owner elects to change it, a UI-level lock and interaction test are needed.
changed_premise: Current Qt code makes the documented divergence directly observable, and a persistent Windows CI probe now covers other parts of §12.2; the ADR’s policy choice itself remains on record.
remaining_work: Keep the deliberate departure distinct in the ledger/feature record. If consistency review changes the policy, lock scaling in each dialog and test an attempted later selection; otherwise preserve the current documented behavior.
